name: Yusuf Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the business tax team at Brightwell Partners, a regional firm with four offices. My clients are owner-run companies: a haulage firm with forty lorries, two garden centres, a family bakery chain. I prepare their year-end accounts and corporation tax returns, and I spend a surprising amount of time on the phone asking where a missing invoice went.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the haulage client, honestly, because the owner Dave knows every lorry by its number plate and the accounts tell a real story. What wears me out is the deadline crunch at the end of each quarter. I use the firm's AI tool now and then, mainly to summarise long contracts, but I double-check everything because I've seen it get a VAT rate wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the AI tool is handy for summaries and that's about it. I'd tell friends the hype was mostly from people selling software. I don't post much, maybe the odd joke in the team chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news for me. My job's steady, I'm well paid for my level, and my girlfriend Lena and I are saving for a house. If AI stays a handy tool, I keep doing tax returns and Lena and I buy a house in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and push for the senior role that opens up next spring. Lena and I would keep putting £1,000 a month into the house deposit. I'd keep using the AI tool for summaries, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the boring, normal future, and I'm fine with boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you even in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, mainly. We've got a good deposit building, but every time we look, the flats near Lena's clinic have gone up again. That's a normal worry, not an AI one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lena do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a physiotherapist at a sports clinic. Her job's all hands and people, so she's never worried about any of this. She teases me about my spreadsheets.

say: The AI tool is **handy for summaries**, and that's about it.
Most of the **hype** came from people **selling software**.
think: It's **good news**: my job's steady and the pay is good for my level.
Lena and I can **buy a house** in about two years.
do: Go for the **senior role** opening up next spring.
Keep putting **£1,000 a month** into the house deposit with Lena.
S0.quote: If AI stays a handy tool, I keep doing tax returns and Lena and I buy a house in two years.
fieldNote: Yusuf's only live worry is **house prices**, which he calls a normal worry.
He uses AI **cautiously**, after seeing it get a VAT rate wrong.
His partner's **hands-on job** gives the household a second, safer income.

steps.text: Apply for the senior business tax role next spring
Put £1,000 a month into the house deposit with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we need training, not just a new tool dropped on us. To friends I'd say accountants will be fine, because someone still has to sign the accounts. I'd mean it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the team shrinks. We've got six people in business tax; in this picture it's maybe four in three years. I'm average at my accounting job, and average people are the ones a firm stops replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for proper AI training and do it seriously, maybe two evenings a week for a few months. Once a few colleagues had used the new tools well, I'd start using them every day too. I'd keep saving for the house but maybe wait a year to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but it'd be on my mind on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say accountants will be fine, but you also think your team shrinks. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Accountants in general will be fine, I think. Whether this accountant is fine depends on whether I'm one of the four. That's the bit I'd keep to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gemma, who's been on the team twelve years and hates new software. She's brilliant with clients but she'd struggle. I'd probably try to help her with the tools.

say: We need **proper training**, not a new tool dropped on us.
Accountants will be fine, because someone still has to **sign the accounts**.
think: The business tax team probably shrinks from **six to four** people.
**Average** staff like me are the ones a firm stops replacing.
do: Take **AI training** two evenings a week for a few months.
Use the tools **daily** once colleagues have shown they work.
Keep saving but **delay buying** the house by about a year.
feel: **Uneasy**, with it on his mind on the drive home.
S1.quote: I'm average at my accounting job, and average people are the ones a firm stops replacing.
fieldNote: Yusuf separates **accountants in general** from himself, and only voices the first in public.
His steady style shows: he'll adopt tools once **others prove them**.
He worries for **Gemma**, an older colleague who dislikes new software.

steps.text: Take the firm's AI training two evenings a week
Push back the house purchase by about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and that governments should've seen it coming. At work I'd ask the partners straight away what the plan is for staff. Online I'd probably share articles rather than say much myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone by 2028 or soon after. Tax returns and accounts are all screen work, so there's no three-year cushion for me. The only good part is Lena's job is hands-on, so she's got until the robots, and maybe longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the house hunt straight away and keep the deposit, about £34,000, as our safety money. I'd start applying for anything that keeps me with clients face to face, like a finance role at the haulage firm, because Dave already likes me. And I'd cut the car lease when it ends in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, properly. We spent three years saving for a house deposit, and now that deposit is what keeps the lights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're okay for money for a while, and that she might be carrying us for a bit. She'd say that's fine. I'd find it harder than she would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the haulage firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Dave's business is lorries and depots, real hands-on stuff, and it'll need someone in the office who knows it. Robots driving lorries are a few years behind. It buys me time while I work out the rest.

say: It's **too fast**, and governments should have seen it **coming**.
I'd ask the partners **straight away** what the plan is for staff.
think: My job's **gone by 2028**, because tax work is all screen work.
Lena's **hands-on job** lasts longer, which is the one good part.
do: Stop the **house hunt** and keep the £34,000 deposit as safety money.
Apply for a **finance role** at the haulage client.
Drop the **car lease** when it ends in March.
feel: **Alarmed**, and uneasy about Lena **carrying** the household.
S2.quote: We spent three years saving for a house deposit, and now that deposit is what keeps the lights on.
fieldNote: Yusuf expects to **lose his job** quickly because his work is all thinking work.
The house deposit turns into an **emergency fund** overnight.
He looks to a client's **hands-on business** as a bridge for a few years.

steps.text: Stop house hunting and keep the £34,000 deposit as emergency savings
Put the house purchase on hold with Lena
Apply for an in-house finance job at the haulage client
Hand back the car lease when it ends in March

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. At work I'd push the firm to tell us which roles they expect to keep. With friends I'd be honest that it worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, like the fast one, my job ends, just later. By 2031 I'd be 32, and I'd want to be somewhere safer before then. Five years is long enough to retrain once, but I wouldn't get a second try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly in year one, because they'd make me useful for the next few years. I'd start a part-time advisory course in year two, aimed at helping owner-run businesses with decisions, not returns. Lena and I would probably still buy, but a cheaper place with a smaller mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's a slow knot rather than a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'a cheaper place' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bed flat instead of the house with a garden we'd wanted, maybe £60,000 less. Lena would grumble about the garden. But a smaller mortgage feels safer if my pay might stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would advisory work really survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. My hope is that business owners like Dave still want a person to talk things through with. But I'd keep watching and be ready to move again.

say: Five years is **enough to get ready** if people start now.
The firm should say **which roles** it expects to keep.
think: My job still **ends**, just later, so I want to move **before 2031**.
There's time to **retrain once**, but not a second time.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly in the first year.
Start a part-time **advisory course** in year two.
Buy a cheaper **two-bed flat** with Lena instead of a house.
feel: **Anxious**, as a slow knot rather than a shock.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to retrain once, but I wouldn't get a second try.
fieldNote: The extra years turn Yusuf's alarm into a **planned** response.
He'd **downsize** the home plans, choosing a smaller mortgage over a garden.
He's honest that he **doesn't know** whether advisory work will survive.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tools properly in the first year
Start a part-time business advisory course in year two
Buy a two-bed flat instead of a house with a garden

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible about it. At work I'd say the firm should train people now and keep the ones it trains. I'd probably say that in the team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is most of my thirties, so I'd get the house, the senior role and a good bit saved. Then I'd need to be out of returns work by around 2034. With ten years of warning, I'd stop being a tax accountant slowly instead of all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the senior role, learn the AI tools as they become normal, and do the advisory qualification over three years. We'd buy the house with the garden, because the pay would last long enough. I'd also put some money into a pension top-up each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. It's a big change, but it's a long road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you speed up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brightwell stopped hiring graduates, I'd take that as the sign. Or if Dave told me he'd stopped needing us because his software does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Her robots are three years behind mine, so in this version she's safe well into the 2030s. We'd probably plan kids for after I've made the switch.

say: There's **time**, so let's be **sensible** about it.
The firm should **train people now** and keep the staff it trains.
think: Ten years covers **most of my thirties**: house, senior role, savings.
I'd need to be out of **returns work** by about 2034.
do: Take the **senior role** and learn AI tools as they become normal.
Do the **advisory qualification** over three years.
Buy the **house with a garden** and top up the pension yearly.
feel: **Uneasy**, but **manageable** because it's a long road.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, I'd stop being a tax accountant slowly instead of all at once.
fieldNote: With a decade, Yusuf expects his **job to end** but on a timeline he controls.
His signal to move would be the firm **stopping graduate hiring**.
The couple would time **children** for after his switch.

steps.text: Take the senior role and learn AI tools as they spread
Complete the business advisory qualification over three years
Buy the house with a garden and plan children later

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd wipe out my work before I'd changed anything. What would help is clear notice from employers, a year at least, and some help paying for retraining. And honestly, cheaper housing, so people like me aren't tied to a big mortgage when the job goes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to couples. In the fast version my girlfriend Lena earns more than me for years, and I'd have to get used to that. I think a lot of people would find that harder than they admit.

headlineQuote: In the fast version my girlfriend Lena earns more than me for years, and I'd have to get used to that.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old tax accountant** at a regional firm, serving owner-run businesses.
He and his partner Lena, a **physiotherapist**, are saving a **£34,000** deposit.
He uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools once others prove them.
He expects his **job to end** under AGI, faster than Lena's hands-on work.
More time lets him **plan**: advisory training, a smaller mortgage, children later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his work would vanish before he'd changed anything.
